End-to-End Model Compression for Personalized Neural Speech Codecs
Inseon Jang1, Minje Kim2, Wootaek Lim1, Seungkwon Beack1
1 Electronics and Telecommunications Research Institute, Daejeon, South Korea
2 University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, Siebel School of Computing and Data Science
jinsn@etri.re.kr, minje@illinois.edu, wtlim@etri.re.kr, skbeack@etri.re.kr
Abstract
Neural speech coding (NSC) leverages deep learning to
achieve high-quality speech compression, surpassing conven-
tional methods. However, recent NSC models have grown sub-
stantially in size and complexity, limiting their feasibility for
real-time processing on resource-constrained devices. To ad-
dress this issue, we propose a speaker-aware model compres-
sion framework for end-to-end NSC. In this approach, speak-
ers are clustered by perceptual similarity, and both encoder and
decoder are trained with group-specific data, reducing compu-
tation while preserving perceptual quality. Subjective listening
tests show that the proposed method reduces the model size by
96% and the bitrate by 50% (from 2 kbps to 1 kbps), while
maintaining the perceptual quality of the state-of-the-art De-
script audio codec (DAC). Moreover, the personalized models
remain robust under noisy conditions, consistently outperform-
ing baselines under acoustic distortions. These results highlight
the feasibility of deploying NSC on low-power devices in both
clean and noisy environments.
Index Terms: Neural speech coding, model compression, per-
sonalization, speech coding
1. Introduction
Neural speech codecs (NSC) are based on deep learning for
effective speech compression and reconstruction, offering su-
perior performance over traditional codecs [1]. Current NSC
methods fall into two categories: neural vocoder–based and
end-to-end codecs. Neural vocoder–based NSCs reconstruct
speech from compressed features using generative vocoders
such as WaveNet [2, 3], WaveRNN [4], LPCNet [5], and HiFi-
GAN [6], which improve perceptual quality at low bitrates with
different trade-offs between quality and efficiency. By contrast,
end-to-end codecs such as SoundStream [7], EnCodec [8], Fun-
Codec [9], and Descript audio codec (DAC) [10] adopt convolu-
tional encoder–decoder architectures with residual vector quan-
tization (RVQ), achieving higher quality at low bitrates. Hybrid
approaches such as SemantiCodec [11] also consider semantic
quality to maximize coding gain.
Advances in NSC have relied heavily on model capacity.
For example, BigCodec uses 159 million parameters, which is
over fifteen times larger than conventional 10M-parameter mod-
els, dramatically increasing computational and memory costs
[12]. SuperCodec employs selective up-/down-sampling, and
SRCodec adds dual attention, both exacerbating computational
overhead [13, 14]. Such demands hinder real-time processing
and limit deployment on low-power devices, emphasizing the
need for model compression and architectural optimization.

Several speaker-agnostic model compression techniques
have been proposed for NSC to reduce computational complex-
ity. Notable approaches include gated residual networks and
depthwise separable convolution [15], sparse matrices applied
to GRUs, and linear prediction for spectral envelope modeling
[5]. A causal architecture using projected Scalar Quantization
and Short-Time Fourier Transform (STFT) representations has
also shown high performance under low-complexity and low-
bitrate conditions [16]. However, these methods are often heav-
ily dependent on specific architectures or have limited compres-
sion, making it difficult to balance model efficiency and percep-
tual quality. To overcome these limitations, more advanced and
generalized model compression approaches are needed.
Personalized neural speech codecs (PNSC) [17] are con-
sidered a promising alternative to speaker-agnostic model com-
pression. PNSC leveragesspeaker-specificcharacteristics by
grouping speakers based on perceptual similarity and training
customized LPCNet vocoder for each group. This approach re-
duces the model complexity while enhancing perceptual qual-
ity at the same bitrate. However, the specific variation proposed
in [17], personalized LPCNet (PLPCNet), applied personaliza-
tion only to the decoder, leaving the non-neural encoder un-
compressed. Since personalization is an architecture-agnostic
concept, PNSC should not be limited to a particular architec-
ture. For example, it can benefit an autoencoder-based codec’s
encoder and decoder synergically. In addition, while PLPC-
Net was validated only on clean speech signals, model person-
alization is reported to be successful in speech enhancement as
shown in personalized speech enhancement models [18, 19].
We propose maximizing the efficacy of personalization by
compressing the encoder, decoder, and quantizer within an
end-to-end framework. To this end, we begin with DAC, a
popular open-sourced neural codec that provides the state-of-

We demonstrate that the personalized DAC (PDAC) model en-
hances speech quality and reduces bitrates and the overall model
complexity. PDAC also shows acceptable robustness to the test
scenario when the test speaker is misclassified into an incorrect
group or contaminated by interfering sources.
2. End-to-End (E2E) Model Compression
for Personalized Neural Speech Codecs
2.1. Overview of the E2E Personalization Scheme for NSC
The proposed end-to-end (E2E) model compression method for
PNSC, both the sender and receiver adapt to speaker-specific
characteristics. It is different from the previous PLPCNet ar-
chitecture [17], which was able to compress only the receiver
portion of the system due to its dependence on the LPCNet
architecture. The proposed E2E compression method is char-
acterized by the sender that extracts speaker-specific features,
classifies the speaker into a pre-defined group, and transmits
both the compressed bitstream and the group index to the re-
ceiver. This group index ensures that the receiver applies the
appropriate personalized decoder as well, resulting in higher re-
construction quality and computational efficiency.
Fig. 1 provides an overview of the E2E personalized codec
system. The input signal is assumed to be a noisy version of a
clean speech, e.g.,x=s+n. It is processed by a noise-robust
speaker encoderF(·)to extract a speaker-specific feature vector
z. Then, it is compared withCpre-defined speaker-group cen-
troids, each of which is representing the speaker-group’s char-
acteristics. The groupc ∗ with the most similar centroid vector
µ(c∗) to the input speaker’s feature vectorzis selected:

where we use Euclidean distance, as the centroids are prepared
based on k-means clustering (more details are in Sec. 2.2).
The input noisy speech signalxis then fed to the separate
noise-robust utterance encoderG (c∗)(·)to produce the com-
pressed bitstreamy:y←G (c∗)(x). Here, the E2E compres-
sion is achieved by exclusively running the small selected en-
coderG (c∗)(·)rather than employing a large general-purpose
speech encoder. Since the sender transmits not onlyybut the
group indexc ∗ to the receiver, the receiver assigns the corre-
sponding personalized decoderD (c∗)(·)for the reconstruction
job: ˆs←D (c∗)(y). Note that the two representationsyand
zserve distinct purposes in the system: the former is the com-
pressed code used for speech reconstruction, whereas the lat-
ter is used solely to classify the speaker into the corresponding
speaker groupc∗. In addition, since the training objective is to
reconstruct the clean speechsfrom the noisy inputx, the codec
as a whole conducts the denoising task. Hence, the bitstreamy
is supposed to contain clean speech’s information rather than
the mixture’s.
The proposed E2E PNSC architecture achieves
personalization-based compression by turning the mix-
ture of local experts (MoLE) architecture [20, 21] into an
exclusive (or sparse) version, where only the relevant local
expert is selected and run during inference instead of their
weighted sum. More specifically, in the proposed system,
since the exclusive MoLE architecture is employed both on the
sender and receiver sides, the model compression effectiveness
increases compared to the existing PLPCNet architecture.

2.2. The Speaker Grouping Strategy
PNSC assumes that a group of speakers with similar speech
characteristics has lower variability than the entire speech cor-
pus. Therefore, differently from conventional deep learning
models that tend to require a large model capacity to general-
ize across extensive data variations, PNSC focuses on a cohe-
sive subset of data, making it possible to use relatively smaller
models.
The speaker grouping is performed in advance in an un-
supervised manner. The speaker encoderF(·)is first trained
to generate discriminative speaker embedding vectorszfrom
noisy speechxso it can handle test-time noisy speech signals
robustly. These embedding vectors are then clustered to define
speaker groups. To be specific, we follow a contrastive learn-
ing approach [22] that leverages the Siamese network architec-
ture, where two noisy speech samplesx i andx j from the same
speaker yield similar embeddings, i.e.,z i ≈z j, while those
from different speakers remain distinguishable. After obtain-
ing the embedding vectors, the k-means clustering algorithm
is applied to the embedding vectors to form speaker groups,
assuming the perceptual similarity between speakers is repre-
sented linearly in the embedding spacez. Similar to [17], this
experiment classifies speakers by identifying the nearest cluster
centroid instead of using a softmax layer as defined in eq. (1).
The main improvement from [17] is that the embeddings are
robust to additive noise.
At the test stage, the classification result (c ∗ in Fig.1)de-
termines the speaker group, which serves as a common refer-
ence for both the encoder and decoder. If the speaker group is
mislabeled, it is possible that the performance of the personal-
ized speech codec could degrade. In Sec. 4, we analyze the
PDAC’s behavior on this issue, where we empirically show that
finetuning of the classification part as well as the local experts
altogether can mitigate the problem.
2.3. Personalized DAC
PDAC is an end-to-end model compression method derived
from the DAC framework. DAC employs a hierarchical en-
coder–decoder with residual vector quantization (RVQ). The
encoder progressively downsamples the input speech using con-
volutional blocks and strides while expanding the channel di-
mension, then applies nonlinear activation and a latent pro-
jection before RVQ compresses the representation. The de-
coder mirrors this process with transposed convolutions to re-
store temporal resolution and reconstruct the waveform, final-
ized with a Tanh activation for perceptual quality.
The dimensionality parameters—encoder dim,
latent dim, anddecoder dim—govern feature diversity
and model capacity. Larger values enhance expressiveness
2537
but increase computational complexity, highlighting the
performance–efficiency trade-off. PDAC addresses this by
personalizing the model to specific speaker groups. Even
with reduced channel sizes, the personalized models capture
group-specific speech traits effectively, lowering complexity
while maintaining quality.
We define theLargemodel as the baseline configura-
tion in the DAC framework, corresponding to a 16kHz sam-
pling rate signal. Based on this structure, we additionally de-
signSmallandTinymodels, where theSmallmodel re-
ducesencoder dim,latent dim, anddecoder dimby
approximately half or more compared to theLargemodel.
Similarly, theTinymodel further reducesencoder dim,
latent dim, anddecoder dimby at least half of the Small
model. The detailed configurations of these models are pre-
sented in Table 1, with their total number of parameters being
74.18M, 14.99M, and 3.02M, respectively.
The proposed PDAC is trained in a group-specific manner:
each personalized encoder-decoder pair{G (c),D (c)}is a spe-
cialized version of the generic DAC model, optimized for the
c-th speaker group.
